FINAL PAYCHECK DEADLINE CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

When is the final paycheck legally due?

Every US state sets its own deadline for paying a departing employee's final paycheck — some require same-day payment when an employee is fired, others allow until the next regular payday, and a handful set a rule in between. This tool applies the deadline for the state and separation type you pick to an actual separation date, and names whether that state requires unused vacation or PTO to be paid out too.

Nothing is uploaded. Your dates and figures are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. State and separation type

California treats notice of 72+ hours the same as a firing — due on your last day worked. Without that notice, the employer has 3 calendar days.

Minnesota's wages become due upon a written demand, with a 24-hour clock from that demand. Without a demand, the deadline is the next regularly scheduled payday instead.

2. Dates

The next scheduled payday is only needed for a next-payday-based rule, and for the "earlier of" rules in Montana, Arizona, and Nevada — leave it blank to see the rule described without an exact date.

3. Accrued vacation/PTO (optional)

Only used to show a dollar figure in states that require vacation/PTO payout as wages — see result below for whether your state is one of them.

Choose a state and separation type, enter a separation date, then click Check.

Result

What this does not cover

  • Not a determination of which state's law governs. This tool applies whichever state you select — it does not decide that for you. That is usually the state where the work was physically performed, which can differ from where the employer is headquartered, especially for a remote employee.
  • No city or county ordinances. Some cities and counties set stricter final-pay rules than their state; none are modeled here.
  • No commissions, bonuses, or expense reimbursement rules. Several states apply separate timing rules to these — not modeled.
  • Eleven states only. Every other state uses the general next-payday default shown above; confirm separately whether that state has since adopted its own statute.
  • Point-in-time figures. State final-pay statutes can change; verify against your state's labor department before relying on a deadline for an actual separation.

Common questions

When is a final paycheck legally due after being fired or laid off?

It depends entirely on the state. California, Colorado, Massachusetts, and Nevada require same-day payment. Montana defaults to immediate but lets a written employer policy extend it to the next payday or 15 days, whichever is sooner. Minnesota starts a 24-hour clock from the employee's written demand. Arizona gives 7 working days or the next payday, whichever is sooner. Texas gives 6 calendar days. Illinois, New York, and Washington all use the next regularly scheduled payday. Most other states have no specific statute and default to the next regular payday.

Does the deadline change if I quit instead of being fired?

In most modeled states, yes — a voluntary quit gets the next regular payday rather than an immediate or same-day deadline. California is the sharpest exception: quitting with at least 72 hours' notice is due on your last day worked, the same as a firing, while quitting without notice gives the employer 3 calendar days.

Is my employer required to pay out my unused vacation or PTO when I leave?

Only in some states. California, Colorado, Massachusetts, Montana, and Illinois treat accrued unused vacation as earned wages that cannot be forfeited, so it must be paid out on the same deadline as the rest of the final paycheck. In every other state modeled here — and in most states generally — payout depends entirely on the employer's written policy or the employment contract, not on a state mandate.

What if my state is not one of the eleven listed?

This tool applies the general default: no state-specific final-paycheck-timing statute was found for that state in this pass, so it follows the next regularly scheduled payday, the practice most sources describe for a state without its own statute. Confirm separately whether that state has since adopted its own rule.

Is this legal advice?

No. This tool applies a published state statute to the dates you enter. It does not determine which state's law actually governs your situation, does not model city or county ordinances that can be stricter than state law, and does not cover commissions, bonuses, or expense reimbursement. It is not a substitute for reviewing current state guidance or consulting a qualified employment attorney or HR compliance professional.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified employment attorney or HR compliance professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming the deadline that actually applies to your situation before acting. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your dates and figures are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (deadline_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Checking whether a call-recording rule applies to a workplace call instead? The call recording consent checker is the one for that — a different state-by-state employment reference, one-party/all-party consent rather than final-pay timing.

Employer sizing up what unused vacation balances cost across the whole team? The PTO accrual liability calculator prices every balance in dollars, projects it to each cap, and applies the payout rule for the state.

Is money being taken out of a paycheck by a garnishment? The wage garnishment limit calculator shows the most federal law lets an order take from a pay stub.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This calculator vs. checking the final-paycheck deadline yourself

Final-paycheck deadlines are not one rule with fifty exceptions. They split three separate ways at once: how fast payment is due, which varies enormously by state; whether being fired or quitting changes that deadline, which it does in some states and not others; and whether accrued vacation must be paid out at all, which follows yet another grouping of states. A manual check that learned one state's answer from experience and reused it elsewhere gets exactly the state that differs wrong.

Where a manual check usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake checking it by handWhat this calculator does
Assuming one payment-speed rule applies everywhereApplying California's same-day rule (or New York's next-payday rule) to every state, when the actual range runs from same-day (CA, CO, MA, NV) to a fixed number of days (TX, MT) to next-payday-only (NY, WA, IL).Applies the specific rule for the state you select, with its own citation.
California's notice-dependent quit ruleTreating every voluntary quit in California the same way, missing that 72+ hours' notice moves the deadline to the last day worked while no notice leaves it at 3 calendar days.Asks whether notice was given and applies the correct one of the two rules.
Minnesota's demand-triggered clockMissing that Minnesota's fast 24-hour deadline only starts once the employee makes a written demand -- without one, the ordinary next-payday rule applies instead.Asks whether a demand was made and applies the 24-hour clock only when it was.
Vacation/PTO payout requirementAssuming the payout rule follows the same state grouping as the payment-speed rule, when it does not -- Texas and Nevada have fast payment deadlines but leave vacation payout to employer policy, while Illinois requires payout regardless of policy.Reports the payout requirement for the selected state independently of its payment-speed rule.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is sent to a server.

Worked example: the same separation date, three different deadlines

The first row is the calculator's own shipped "load an example" scenario -- open the calculator and click it to see the same numbers.

ScenarioDeadlineVacation/PTO payout required?
California, voluntary quit, no 72-hour notice, separated Oct 1, 2026, 40 accrued hours at $28/hourSun, Oct 4, 2026 (3 calendar days after separation)Yes -- $1,120.00 at the hours/rate entered
Same facts, but 72+ hours' notice givenThu, Oct 1, 2026 (the day of separation)Yes -- California requires it regardless of notice
New York, fired/laid off, separated Oct 1, 2026, next payday Oct 10, 2026Sat, Oct 10, 2026 (the next regularly scheduled payday)No -- New York leaves it to employer policy

Three days apart on payment speed, three days apart again once notice changes, and a payout answer that has nothing to do with either. A hand check that got the first row right by applying "3 days" has no way to know the second row is "same day" unless it separately remembered the notice carve-out, and no way to know the third row's payout answer without separately checking that New York's rule, unlike California's, leaves it to the employer.

Common questions

Is the final-paycheck deadline the same in every state?

No, and the range is wide. California, Colorado, Massachusetts, and Nevada require same-day or immediate payment for a firing or layoff. New York, Washington, and Illinois require only the next regularly scheduled payday -- no shorter statutory deadline at all. A manual check that learned the rule from experience in one state and applied it to an employee in another gets it wrong in either direction: too strict where the actual rule is looser, or too late where it is stricter.

Does California's deadline for a voluntary quit depend on anything besides the state?

Yes -- whether the employee gave at least 72 hours' notice before quitting, and this is the detail most likely to be missed by hand. An employee who gives 72+ hours' notice must be paid on their last day worked, the same as a firing. An employee who quits without that notice has 3 calendar days instead. Treating every voluntary quit in California the same way, regardless of notice, gets one of the two cases wrong.

Why would a manual check assume every state requires vacation payout, or that none do?

Because the rule genuinely splits by state with no obvious pattern tied to the payment-deadline rule itself. California, Colorado, Massachusetts, Montana, and Illinois require accrued unused vacation to be paid out as wages, with no use-it-or-lose-it forfeiture. New York, Washington, Texas, Arizona, Nevada, and Minnesota leave it entirely to employer policy -- there is no state mandate either way. A manual check that assumes the payout answer follows the same state grouping as the payment-speed rule will get several states backwards, since the two rules do not track each other.

What is easy to miss about Minnesota's final-paycheck rule specifically?

That the fast deadline is triggered by a written demand, not by the firing itself. Without a demand, a fired Minnesota employee's wages are due on the next regular payday, the same as most states. Once the employee makes a written demand for payment, the employer has only 24 hours from that demand. A check that applies the 24-hour clock to every Minnesota firing, or misses that the clock exists at all, gets the deadline wrong depending on which half it skipped.

If I get the deadline right, have I fully determined what the employer owes?

No. This is a payment-timing and vacation-payout lookup, not a full wage-and-hour determination. It does not determine which state's law actually governs (usually the state where the work was performed, which can differ from where the employer is headquartered), does not model city or county ordinances that can be stricter than state law, and does not cover commissions, bonuses, or expense reimbursement rules.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply published state final-pay-timing statutes to the dates and facts you supply. They are not legal, tax, or financial advice, and do not replace a qualified employment attorney or HR compliance professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying the output before relying on it, and for confirming the deadline that actually applies to your situation before acting. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.
